content: 1. The quality of the studies was not assessed using the QUADAS-2 tool or the STARD checklist, as these were deemed inapplicable to the context of the analysis. 2. None of the studies met the inclusion criteria for the systematic review, and therefore, a GRADE summary of findings was not applicable. 3. Predictive modeling analysis by Public Health England demonstrated that the prevalence of the condition and the specificity of the assay significantly influence the positive predictive value (PPV). For example, when a test with relatively low sensitivity (<99%) is used, the ratio of true positives to false positives is high, but the PPV decreases. 4. In all but the highest population prevalence settings, the use of less sensitive test kits in a two-test strategy had only a modest impact on negative predictive values (NPVs). However, calculations showed that substantial diagnostic accuracy gains could be achieved with a modest investment in a second, independent test kit for initially reactive individuals. 5. Predictive modeling analysis by Boston University (Linas) is to be added at a later meeting. 6. The use of a single test on one anti-HCV/core antigen assay simplifies the testing process, reduces overall costs, and allows for faster reporting of results, enabling timely follow-up for further assessment or health protection advice. 7. However, a single test strategy may reduce the PPV, leading to more false positives, particularly in low-prevalence settings. This could result in unnecessary follow-up testing or treatment, causing anxiety and additional costs. 8. A survey conducted by FIND in September 2015 among 104 respondents from 43 countries (20 high-income and 23 lowand middle-income) revealed that 50% of respondents from lowand middle-income settings preferred a one-assay screening strategy before confirmatory testing. 9. Patients require a simple, rapid testing strategy that is acceptably accurate for the purpose of diagnosis. 10. Health-care workers need to understand the strengths and limitations of any given testing strategy to appropriately counsel patients and act on the results, whether positive or negative. 11. Laboratory staff must be adequately trained to perform various assays according to manufacturers’ instructions. 12. The availability of HCV RNA NAT assays or supplemental testing, such as core antigen testing, is more accessible in settings with established hepatitis C testing facilities, raising equity concerns. 13. NAT assays are highly sensitive and specific but are more expensive than serological methods like HCV core antigen testing. They also require sophisticated laboratory equipment and skilled staff. 14. HCV core antigen testing was developed as an alternative to NAT for diagnosing active HCV infection. It detects nucleocapsid peptides (p22) released into plasma during viral assembly and can be detected throughout the course of infection. 15. HCV core antigen testing is detectable earlier than antibodies and has been applied as an additional analyte in serological assays to ascertain exposure to HCV. 16. Both HCV core antigen and HCV RNA (qualitative or quantitative) have clinical utility for detecting active HCV infection, though there is limited research comparing these methods. 17. A threshold of >10,000 IU/mL captures 95% of persistent HCV infections, except for a minority with partial viral control. 18. Systematic reviews were commissioned to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of HCV core antigen testing and qualitative versus quantitative RNA methods for diagnosing active HCV infection. 19. The lower limit of detection for most commercial qualitative NAT assays is 10–15 IU/mL, while for quantitative assays, it is 600–1100 IU/mL. 20. Newer quantitative viral load assays report detection limits similar to qualitative assays but may not quantify results at that level. 21. NAT assays for detection on capillary whole blood and dried blood spots are being developed to increase accessibility. 22. HCV core antigen assays have been commercialized as standalone tests or in combination with antibody assays to improve sensitivity in early infection. However, these assays do not differentiate seropositivity from active infection. 23. The addition of core antigen in combination assays was intended to increase sensitivity in early infection, but the purpose is not to distinguish between antigen and antibody detection. 24. Draft recommendations include further research on the use of HCV core antigen as a one-stop diagnostic test and the impact of one-test versus two-test screening strategies on hepatitis C testing services. 25. The diagnostic accuracy of HCV core antigen testing varies across different prevalence settings, with sensitivity and specificity influenced by the assay used. 26. The systematic review highlights the need for appropriate follow-up procedures to address false positives in one-assay strategies and improve the overall testing strategy’s PPV.
